props.title: Flubber

sections.content: Flubber reimagines Disney's classic The Absent-Minded Professor (1961) with Robin Williams bringing his signature manic energy to the role of Professor Philip Brainard. The film exemplifies late-90s family sci-fi comedy, blending practical effects with then-cutting-edge CGI to bring the green bouncing substance to life. While not reaching the heights of Williams' other family films like Mrs. Doubtfire (1993) or Jumanji (1995), Flubber captures that distinctly Disney approach to slapstick science fiction that defined films like Honey, I Shrunk the Kids (1989).

sections.content: The late 90s saw a surge of science-themed family comedies that mixed wonder with slapstick humor. Inspector Gadget (1999) brought the cartoon detective to life with similar energy, while My Favorite Martian (1999) attempted to recapture classic sci-fi comedy. These films shared Flubber's emphasis on visual effects and physical comedy, though often at the expense of the more grounded emotional storytelling found in earlier entries like Back to the Future (1985).

Robin Williams' performance as Professor Brainard follows a tradition of eccentric movie scientists, from Christopher Lloyd's Doc Brown to Rick Moranis in Honey, I Shrunk the Kids (1989). The character type combines intellectual brilliance with social awkwardness, using science as both a source of comedy and wonder. This archetype continues in modern family films like Big Hero 6 (2014), though with more emotional depth and contemporary sensibilities. SUBHEAD: The Evolution of Disney Science Comedy

sections.content: Flubber represents a transitional period in Disney's approach to science-based family entertainment. While earlier films like The Computer Wore Tennis Shoes (1969) relied primarily on practical effects and simple premises, Flubber embraced CGI technology while maintaining physical comedy elements. This hybrid approach influenced later Disney science comedies like Sky High (2005) and Meet the Robinsons (2007), which further developed the balance between effects-driven spectacle and character-driven storytelling.
